course.title: Camday – Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics — Stage 9

unit.title: Angles
unit.blurb: Angles with parallel lines and in triangles, interior and exterior angles of polygons, ruler-and-compass constructions and Pythagoras' theorem.
unit.subject: maths

O1.t: Calculate angles using angle facts: angles on a line, around a point, in a triangle, and alternate, corresponding and co-interior angles.

O2.t: Derive and use the sum of the interior angles of a polygon.

O3.t: Use the sum of exterior angles of a polygon (360°) to find angles and the number of sides of regular polygons.

O4.t: Describe and use ruler-and-compass constructions: perpendicular bisector, angle bisector and the perpendicular from a point to a line.

O5.t: Use Pythagoras' theorem to find a missing side of a right-angled triangle and solve problems.

p: A carpenter builds a roof truss: two parallel beams are joined by a sloping strut. One angle is marked **64°**, and the truss also contains an isosceles triangle.
Which angle facts would you need to find all the other angles? Think about it before you read on.
Straight line 180°; around a point 360°; vertically opposite angles are equal; triangle 180°; quadrilateral 360°.

p: Where a line crosses two parallel lines: **corresponding** angles are equal (F shape), **alternate** angles are equal (Z shape), and **co-interior** angles add to 180° (C shape).
Real problems need a **chain** of facts. Write the reason for each step, e.g. 'alternate angles', 'angles in a triangle', 'base angles of an isosceles triangle'.
In an isosceles triangle the two base angles are equal; in a parallelogram opposite angles are equal and neighbouring angles add to 180°.

Step 4: Continue until you reach the angle you need.

p: From one vertex, diagonals split a polygon with **n sides** into **n − 2 triangles**. So the sum of the interior angles is **(n − 2) × 180°**.
In a **regular** polygon every angle is equal, so each interior angle = **(n − 2) × 180° ÷ n**.
Octagon: 1080 ÷ 8 = **135°**. Two octagons meet with 270° at a point, leaving 90° – a square fills the gap.

p: A design student must draw a **regular hexagon** logo and some **60°, 30° and 45°** guide lines – using only a ruler and compasses (no protractor).
How could circles help you make exact angles? Think about it before you read on.
An angle bisector splits an angle in half; a perpendicular bisector meets a line at 90° through its midpoint.
**60°**: draw a line AB. With compasses at A, draw an arc crossing AB at C. With the same radius at C, draw an arc crossing the first arc at D. Angle DAC = 60° (triangle ACD is equilateral).
**30°**: bisect the 60° angle.
**45°**: construct a perpendicular (90°), then bisect it.
Leave all construction arcs visible – they show your method.
**Hexagon**: draw a circle. Keep the compasses at the same radius and step round the circle, marking 6 points. Join them. (Each side equals the radius.)
**Square**: draw a diameter, construct its perpendicular bisector (another diameter). The 4 ends are the vertices.
**Octagon**: bisect the right angles between the square's diameters to get 8 points.
Drawing a polygon with its vertices on a circle is called **inscribing** it.
